blurb: Mixture of experts, cheaper attention, state space models and the rise of small models.

cards.title: Only wake the experts you need

steps.p: An MoE layer replaces one feed-forward network with many "experts" — say 8, 64 or 256.
For each token, a small router picks the top few experts, and only those run.
Total parameters can be enormous while the compute per token matches a much smaller dense model.

cards.aside: Many leading models are now believed or confirmed to be MoE.

cards.q: Mixtral 8×7B has about 47B parameters, not 56B, because…
options: Attention and embedding layers are shared — only the MLPs are duplicated into experts
cards.why: Shared non-expert layers. Only the feed-forward blocks are multiplied. With two experts active per token, about 13B parameters do work per token.

cards.statement: In MoE language models, each expert typically specializes in a human-recognizable subject like biology or law.
cards.why: False. Analyses, including of Mixtral, found little clean topic specialization. Routing often follows syntax, token types or position instead.

cards.q: DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total parameters but activates about 37B per token. Roughly what fraction is active?
cards.why: About 5.5%. 37 ÷ 671. Very sparse activation is how it achieved strong performance at relatively low training cost.

cards.title: Google's Switch Transformer (2021) routed each token to just one expert and scaled to 1.6 trillion parameters.
cards.detail: Earlier work used two or more experts per token. Switch showed one was enough, simplifying routing and cutting communication.

cards.statement: An MoE model needs less GPU memory than a dense model with the same number of active parameters.
cards.why: False. All experts must be loaded, since any token might need any of them. MoE saves compute, not memory.

cards.title: Shrinking the KV cache

steps.p: Grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key-value head, shrinking the cache by that ratio.
Sliding-window attention limits each token to a recent window, capping per-layer cost.
DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention stores keys and values in a small compressed vector, rebuilding them as needed.

cards.aside: The KV cache, not the weights, often limits how many users a GPU can serve.

options: KV cache size, by having groups of query heads share key and value heads
cards.why: KV cache. Llama 2 70B uses 64 query heads but only 8 key-value heads, an 8× smaller cache with little quality loss.

cards.statement: With sliding-window attention, information can still travel further than the window by passing through several layers.
cards.why: True. Each layer extends reach by one window, like a relay. Twenty layers with a 4,000-token window can in principle carry information much further.

cards.title: DeepSeek-V2's latent attention cut its KV cache by about 93% compared with its previous model.
cards.detail: By caching a compressed latent vector instead of full keys and values, it could serve far longer contexts and larger batches on the same hardware.

options: Reduce attention's cost from growing with n² to growing with n
cards.why: Linear scaling. Reformulating attention can avoid comparing every pair of tokens, though usually with some loss in exact recall.

cards.q: Which problem does grouped-query attention NOT solve?
options: The quadratic cost of computing attention scores over long prompts
cards.why: Quadratic scoring remains. Every query still scores every key. GQA shrinks what is stored and read, not the number of comparisons.

cards.title: RNNs, reinvented

steps.p: State space models carry a fixed-size state forward through the sequence, like an RNN.
Clever math lets them train in parallel across the sequence, avoiding the RNN slowdown.
Mamba (2023) made the state update depend on the input, letting it choose what to remember or forget.

cards.aside: No growing KV cache: generation cost per token stays constant regardless of context length.

cards.q: The key inference advantage of Mamba-style models is…
options: Constant memory and time per generated token, no matter how long the context
cards.why: Constant cost per token. Transformers' KV caches grow with context. An SSM's state stays fixed, which suits very long inputs.

cards.statement: Pure state space models match transformers at copying long exact strings from earlier in the context.
cards.why: False. A fixed-size state cannot hold everything exactly. Transformers can look back at any token directly, so they win at precise recall.

cards.q: Why do hybrid models mix attention layers with Mamba layers?
options: Attention provides precise recall; SSM layers provide efficiency
cards.why: Best of both. A few attention layers handle exact lookups while most layers stay cheap. Examples include AI21's Jamba and NVIDIA's Nemotron-H.

cards.title: Mamba was created by Albert Gu and Tri Dao — who also invented FlashAttention.
cards.detail: Tri Dao thus helped make transformers faster and also build one of their most prominent challengers.

cards.statement: RWKV is a recurrent architecture that can be trained in parallel like a transformer.
cards.why: True. An open-source project, RWKV runs like an RNN at inference but uses a formulation that trains in parallel.

cards.title: Doing more with less

steps.p: A small student model learns to imitate a large teacher's outputs.
Unneeded weights are removed and the rest stored in fewer bits.
Carefully curated and synthetic data packs more learning into each parameter.

cards.aside: Small models run on phones and laptops: private, offline and nearly free per query.

cards.q: Apple's on-device foundation model, announced in 2024, has about how many parameters?
cards.why: About 3 billion, small enough to run on an iPhone. Harder requests go to larger models on Apple's private cloud servers.

cards.statement: Pruning can remove a significant share of a network's weights with only a small loss in quality.
cards.why: True. Many weights contribute little. The challenge is turning that sparsity into real speedups on hardware built for dense math.

cards.q: In knowledge distillation, a student learns from the teacher's full probability distribution because…
options: It shows how the teacher ranks wrong answers too, which carries extra information
cards.why: "Dark knowledge". Knowing that a picture is a bit dog-like but not at all car-like teaches more than a single hard label.

cards.title: The 2015 paper that named "knowledge distillation" was co-written by Geoffrey Hinton and Jeff Dean.
cards.detail: With Oriol Vinyals, they showed a small model trained on a big model's softened output probabilities could capture much of its ability.

cards.title: Run a small model on your own laptop
cards.body: Ollama (from ollama.com, and the tool this app's card pipeline will use) runs small models of a few billion parameters comfortably on most laptops, offline and free.
cards.challenge: Install Ollama, then in PowerShell run: ollama run llama3.2:3b — ask it something from today's lessons and judge the answer.
